extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, USPTO officials, policymakers, and patent litigators
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of statutory and procedural standards from a legislative committee report describing proposed changes to patent law, USPTO practice, venue, claim construction appeals, inequitable conduct, applicant submissions, fee authority, and related remedies. Intended to guide practitioners and policymakers on compliance and litigation strategy under the proposed Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of applications (18-month publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocated publication of all patent applications and elimination of the secrecy exception; recommendation to require publication of all patent applications 18 months after filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication promotes the disclosure purpose of the patent system, minimizes uncertainty associated with submarine patents, increases business certainty, promotes rational planning, and reduces unanticipated 'submarine patents' used to hold up competitors for royalties. (Cites NAS and FTC recommendations and related Congressional testimony.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party submissions may include relevance statements
rubrics_metrics.description: After an application is published, third parties may submit relevant prior art; the Act improves the process by permitting third parties to make statements concerning the relevance of patents, patent applications, and other printed publications they submit to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current rules (35 C.F.R. Sec. 1.99) limited submissions to patents/publications and precluded explanation of relevancy; allowing explanations increases the value of submissions to examiners and may reduce deterrence to submitting relevant prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue: proper fora for suing defendants in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendants in patent cases may be sued where the defendant has its principal place of business, or where it is incorporated or formed; they may also be sued where substantial acts of infringement occur, but only if the defendant also has a regular and established, substantial physical facility in that district, which the defendant controls, and which constitutes a substantial portion of the defendant’s overall operations in the district.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This amendment limits district-venue availability compared to the then-prevailing broad interpretations (VE Holding, Beverly Hills Fan) that led to venue wherever personal jurisdiction existed. It is intended to reduce forum-shopping and ensure cases are brought where the defendant has significant contacts and where evidence/witnesses are located.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on manufacturing venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties will not be permitted to manufacture venue (for example, by incorporating in a State simply to establish venue there).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act prevents a company from establishing venue in a given State merely by incorporating there; venue must be based on genuine ties such as principal place, incorporation, or substantial controlled physical facility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special venue exception for universities, non-profits, and small inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Revised section 1400 creates an exception permitting individual inventors, institutions of higher education, and technology-transfer non-profit organizations affiliated with such institutions to file patent infringement or declaratory judgment actions in the district where they reside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee is sensitive to unique position of these parties; the exception is intended to avoid burdensome venue restrictions for entities with limited resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same venue rules for declaratory judgment and infringement cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The Committee determined that the same venue rules shall apply for both patent declaratory judgment cases and patent infringement cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change addresses prior application of different standards in declaratory judgment contexts and aims for parity between claim types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited requests for transfer of venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1400 provides for limited requests for transfer of venue where the court deems it appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts retain authority to transfer venue in appropriate circumstances to further convenience and the interests of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue for foreign defendants with U.S. subsidiaries
rubrics_metrics.description: A foreign defendant that has a U.S. subsidiary may only be sued where its primary U.S. subsidiary is located, or its principal place of business in the U.S. is incorporated or formed. Section 1391(d) continues to determine venue for a foreign defendant that does not have a subsidiary in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies and limits where foreign entities can be haled into U.S. district courts for patent cases, tying venue to the U.S. presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory appeals of claim construction (Markman) — district court certification
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 8 amends 28 U.S.C. §1292(c)(2) to give district court judges discretion to certify Markman claim construction orders for interlocutory review; when such orders are certified, the Federal Circuit must decide the appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfers discretion from Federal Circuit to district court judge to determine whether and when an interlocutory appeal of claim construction would best promote case resolution. The district court may also stay the case pending appeal. Rationale: district judges are best positioned to know when the case is ready for appellate claim construction resolution; intended to reduce costs and increase predictability given high reversal rates on claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant quality submissions — Director authority to require search reports and explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11 gives the Director express authority to require by regulation the submission of search reports and other relevant information as the Director determines; failure to comply shall constitute abandonment of the applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: many applications contain no prior art while others dump many references without explanation; requiring applicants to search and explain prior art will improve the quality of issued patents and assist examiners. The Director may set procedures and exemptions by regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro-entity exemption from applicant submission requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act defines 'micro-entity' (true, independent inventors) and exempts micro-entities from the requirement of submitting the search reports and other information that the Director may require under Section 11.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee expects the USPTO to make further accommodations recognizing the special status and limited resources of micro-entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct — codified standard and safeguards (new 35 U.S.C. §298)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 12 inserts a new §298 that codifies and clarifies the doctrine of inequitable conduct: (a) requires proof by clear and convincing evidence; (b) defines 'material' as information a reasonable examiner would consider important in deciding whether to allow the patent application (non-cumulative information important in deciding whether to allow the patent); (c) permits intent to deceive to be inferred but not solely on the basis of gross negligence or on materiality alone; (d) requires that inequitable conduct claims be pled with particularity under Rule 9(b); (e) grants the court discretion to fashion appropriate remedies, which can include holding one, more than one, or all claims unenforceable and/or denying equitable relief such as injunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses problems of multiple materiality standards, inference of intent from materiality alone, and the all-or-nothing remedy. Aims to balance applicants’ duty of candor with not chilling meaningful disclosures to the USPTO. Pleading and evidentiary requirements should reduce harassment via over-pleading inequitable conduct defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to accept late filings (unintentional delay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 13 expands the Director’s authority to accept any late-filed applications or other filings if the filer satisfies the Director that the delay was unintentional. Any request must be filed within 30 days of the missed deadline and must demonstrate that the delay was unintentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director has discretion to grant such requests and the Director’s decision is not appealable. This broadens existing limited revival/reinstatement authorities (e.g., 35 U.S.C. §§41, 111, 133) to allow more flexibility for unintentional delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO fee-setting authority and public process
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 9 allows the USPTO Director to set or adjust all patent and trademark fees so long as they reasonably compensate the USPTO for services performed; fees shall be prescribed by rule with required consultation with PPAC/TPAC, publication of proposed fee changes in the Federal Register including specific rationale, and a public comment period of not less than 45 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director must give notice to and receive input from the Patent or Trademark Public Advisory Committees, provide public hearings, disseminate recommendations publicly, and notify the Chair and Ranking Member of the Senate and House Judiciary Committees of any final fee decisions. Congress shall have no more than 45 days to consider and comment on any proposed fee, and no proposed fee shall be effective prior to expiration of the 45-day period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue for challenging USPTO decisions updated to current USPTO residence
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the USPTO now resides in the Eastern District of Virginia, sections authorizing venue for litigation against the USPTO are changed to reflect the USPTO's current residence rather than the District of Columbia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congressional housekeeping change to make statutory venue references uniform with the agency’s actual location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residency restriction for Federal Circuit judges eliminated
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10 eliminates the requirement that Federal Circuit judges reside within 50 miles of the District of Columbia by repealing the relevant portion of subsection 44(c) of title 28.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee believes removing this restriction allows a nationwide talent pool for selecting judges; duty stations of the Federal Circuit judges remain in D.C., and travel arrangements are analogous to regional circuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on remedies for Check 21 compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Congress has mandated implementation of the Check 21 Act, the Committee accepted an amendment declaring that practicing the Check 21 industry standard should not constitute patent infringement. Section 14 amends 35 U.S.C. §287 to limit remedies available against a financial institution with respect to a check imaging and archival method or system that is called for under the Check 21 Act, applying to civil actions pending or filed on or after enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits damages and other remedies against financial institutions implementing statutorily required check imaging methods, while not impacting other uses of those methods or systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant assistance expectation: disclose/search relevant prior art with explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are expected to perform initial searches and disclose relevant prior art and explain how it applies; dumping many references without explanation or providing no prior art is unhelpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximately 25% of applications contain no prior art disclosure and another 25% cite twenty or more references with little or no explanation. Requiring applicants to search and explain will improve examination quality because applicants are often best positioned to know relevant art.
